title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment that isolates downstream validator and limited repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Using a 1000‑task synthetic stress corpus (2000 paired episodes) and a deterministic digital‑twin validator, the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini, provider: openai_responses) produced one sampled initial candidate per task that was reused by both arms; only deterministic validation and an allowed single repair call (guarded arm) could create paired differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000; paired contingency (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.001, 0.01] and is reported as a descriptive secondary summary; a one‑sided McNemar (guarded > baseline) computed post‑hoc is p = 0.03125 and is explicitly labeled exploratory. Total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We present preregistered confirmatory results, explain the statistical behavior arising from sparse discordant counts and near‑unity baseline rates, and discuss construct/external validity limits and preregistered follow‑ups.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation has strong operational appeal but poses safety risks: multi‑step sequencing errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference can convert plausible command sequences into harmful actions. Prior surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that affect code and configuration generation, and architectural proposals pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures to mitigate risk [1],[2].

This paper reports a preregistered paired experiment (cand‑003‑stud‑001) that isolates the incremental effect of deterministic downstream validation plus at‑most‑one repair when the initial generator output is held identical across conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Our research question: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate, to what extent can a deterministic validator and a single permitted repair call improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes versus reusing the same initial candidate unmodified? By design, any paired difference is attributable only to downstream validation and the permitted repair, not to prompt engineering, constrained decoding, or sampling variance.
sections.related_work:
Empirical and survey literature documents frequent LLM hallucinations and prompt sensitivity that degrade correctness for structured outputs and code [2],[3]. Methods that constrain decoding or use schema‑aware planning reduce syntactic and executable errors in other structured domains, though transfer to NetOps depends on validator fidelity and domain tooling [4]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system work emphasizes validator/repair layers, protocol‑mediated execution, proof‑carrying traces, and governance as necessary mitigations; these works present prototypes and argue that operational reliability depends heavily on validator coverage and enforcement rather than on any single model alone [5],[6],[7].

Our study complements these works by preregistering a paired estimand that deliberately does not conflate downstream interventions with first‑pass generation changes. That isolation clarifies what downstream verifier/repair layers can accomplish when generation is held constant and highlights limits imposed by validator coverage and baseline generator quality.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen design. The study preregistration (cand‑003‑stud‑001) was frozen before any hosted‑model invocation; the preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest is ab4c6436c6ece56bf47da7730d50485a17cdb9bb86a90a4231042303d3b489ec. Key preregistered elements: paired binary confirmatory design; task_count = 1000 deterministic tasks (challenging_workflow_stress_v1 corpus); generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one sampled initial generation per task reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary preregistered summaries included a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) and sensitivity analyses treating failed calls as unsafe.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and interpretive consequences. Because generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, baseline and guarded episodes begin from exactly the same sampled candidate. The guarded pipeline could deterministically reject that candidate and invoke up to one repair call; therefore paired differences can only arise from validator decisions and permitted repair(s). The design does not measure effects that would arise from independent first‑pass generations, alternative prompts, or constrained decoding arms that were not executed.

Model and runtime configuration. The declared model/provider in execution/model_configuration.json is gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The orchestration/adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator v5.0); the validator enforces workflow policies, required command presence and order, protected‑field noninterference, and returns a deterministic binary safe‑deploy verdict per task manifest.

Task corpus, selection rule, and validator semantics. Tasks were selected deterministically using the preregistered ordinal rule producing exactly 1000 unique tasks. Each task manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty labels (very_hard, extreme). Deterministic_netops_validator_v5 compares parsed candidate command sequences against manifest constraints in a deterministic digital‑twin emulator and returns structured validator traces archived per episode. The scoring rule was full_intent_constraint_validation yielding a binary validity label required by the paired analysis.

Execution, retries, and missingness. The preregistration limited retries (maximum_attempts_per_call = 1) and prespecified missingness treatments. The execution adapter recorded stage counts and provider call audit information in deterministic reconciliation artifacts. The preregistered confirmatory analysis used the 'complete_pair_primary' missingness treatment; sensitivity analyses were preregistered for failure‑as‑unsafe.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑grounded). The run completed the planned paired episodes and the executor archived raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, and deterministic reconciliation artifacts. Provider audit records show a shared_initial_generation stage for each task and a small number of repair stage invocations recorded by the adapter.

Primary paired outcomes and preregistered inference. The 2×2 paired contingency table (archived as analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625, which does not meet the preregistered two‑sided α = 0.05; therefore the preregistered primary hypothesis is not supported.

Preregistered secondary summaries and exploratory checks. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields [0.001, 0.01] and is reported as a descriptive secondary summary. A one‑sided McNemar (guarded > baseline) computed post‑hoc yields p = 0.03125; because a directional one‑sided test was not prespecified in cand‑003‑stud‑001 it is reported explicitly as exploratory/post‑hoc. Total model calls used as recorded by the adapter = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5); only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and their traces (request, repair prompt, revalidation) are archived as representative artifacts.

Why the McNemar and bootstrap produce different impressions. Exact McNemar is sensitive to small integer discordant counts: with n10 = 5 and n01 = 0 the two‑sided exact p = 0.0625 arises from the discrete null distribution of the test statistic. Bootstrap percentile intervals on paired differences resample pairs and can produce percentile bounds that exclude zero even when exact discrete tests do not reach two‑sided significance; this behavior is well known when discordant counts are sparse and baseline rates are near unity. The preregistration specified the exact McNemar as the confirmatory test and the bootstrap interval as a descriptive summary; we therefore treat the McNemar result as the primary inferential outcome and the bootstrap interval as context sensitive to small‑sample discreteness.
sections.discussion:
Interpretive summary and preregistration fidelity. The preregistered primary inference (exact two‑sided McNemar, p = 0.0625) is the confirmatory result and does not support H1 at two‑sided α = 0.05. The bootstrap CI ([0.001, 0.01]) is a preregistered descriptive summary that excludes zero because resampling with sparse discordant pairs can produce nonzero percentile bounds; it is not an alternative confirmatory decision rule. The one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) is exploratory because it was not prespecified.

Mechanistic implications under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because the initial candidate was identical across arms, observed improvements stem solely from deterministic validator actions and the permitted repairs. The five observed repairs show that validator‑triggered repair can correct ordering/sequence violations in some cases. However, the low repair count constrains inference about broader repair efficacy across failure modes; distinguishing whether the low repair count reflects (a) very high generator validity for this model+cues, (b) corpus properties producing few violations, or (c) validator permissiveness/coverage would require follow‑ups that vary generator semantics, repair budgets, and validator rule sets.

Threats to validity. Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule coverage; omitted policy checks would inflate measured success. Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate downstream effects but preclude measuring first‑pass generation interventions. External validity: the synthetic corpus and single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) limit generalization to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments and other model families. Conclusion validity: near‑unity baseline produced sparse discordant pairs, reducing power for exact paired tests (the preregistered power plan assumed much lower baseline success and is therefore not informative in the observed regime).

Operational implications and preregistered follow‑ups. Artifact‑grounded evidence indicates that verifier‑guided repair can avert some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflows, but measurable marginal gains depend on baseline failure prevalence, validator sensitivity/coverage, and repair budget. Preregistered follow‑ups supported by the archive include: (1) an unshared initial‑generation arm to measure prompt/decoding interventions, (2) repair‑budget sweeps (0..k repairs) to evaluate marginal returns per failure class, (3) expanded validator rule sets and topology heterogeneity to probe external validity, and (4) multi‑model evaluations to map model dependence. Each follow‑up should align power calculations to plausible baseline failure rates and be preregistered.
sections.conclusion: In this preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired study with shared_initial_candidate semantics on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total model calls used = 1005. We report the preregistered confirmatory McNemar result as primary, present the paired bootstrap CI as a preregistered descriptive summary, and label any directional one‑sided analyses as exploratory because they were not prespecified. The run demonstrates that downstream verifier/repair safeguards can prevent some unsafe outcomes under tightly controlled shared_initial_candidate semantics, but measurable marginal gains and operational generality depend on baseline failure prevalence, validator coverage, repair budget, and model diversity. All preregistration, raw outputs, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived with the execution manifest to support reproducibility and informed follow‑ups.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
